newsitem.title: USA: Despite floods, some won't leave Kentucky home.
newsitem.headline: Despite floods, some won't leave Kentucky home.

text.p: With the flooding Ohio River already lapping at the rooftops of many downtown businesses, police and military officials told each of the 65 residents, who until then had refused to evacuate their homes, that it was time to leave.
Although some of the approximately 20 families still in their homes heeded the advice, most did not.
"Some people just don't want to come out," said Mililani Chun, spokesperson for the Hardin County Disaster and Emergency Services.
"Yesterday we were in a speedboat and we ran across a man who was fishing from his backyard," said Chun.
Eddie Moore of the Westpoint Volunteer Fire Department said the family his crew went to warn weren't about to leave.

"We went out to check on a farm two miles out of town," he said. "They were okay. They have heat and there isn't water in the basement. They have food and water and a boat. There was an elderly woman there. She said she has lived through two floods before and she is going to live through this one. She was not going to leave her house."

Moore, who's home and wife's business have been flooded, said he explained to the family that after Thursday night, they'd be on their own in the event of an emergency, since officials were going to relocate to nearby Radcliff.

Unlike hard-hit cities like Shepherdsville and Lebanon Junction which were severely flooded by tributary rivers that have already crested, the main threat to West Point comes from the Ohio River itself which is expected to crest Friday evening at 70.4 feet.

Chief of Police Carlos Cintron said Thursday afternoon when the evacuation order was issued that it was time for people, even those few still on dry land, to leave the city -- which was accessible by boat or military vehicle only.

"I think it is important that they come out," he said. "What happens when night falls and there is an emergency? If the Coast Guard leaves and the National Guard leaves because of the rising water, we won't have any way to get those people out. The current out there is very strong."
But the water, Chun said, is still slowly but steadily rising.
